implementation_notes: A document is a record or class with init-only properties and System.Text.Json does the wire work: JsonSerializer.Serialize/Deserialize (string, stream and UTF-8 overloads) together with JsonSerializerOptions for property naming, null, number and field handling, JsonPropertyName to pin wire names, JsonInclude where a field must be published, and JsonConstructor or positional record parameters to bind immutable documents. That replaces the classic hand-written message class: the record is the document type, the serializer is the codec, and the endpoint deserializes, validates and then decides. Source-generated JsonSerializerContext metadata is the trim- and AOT-safe route, JsonDocument/JsonNode covers documents whose shape is only known at runtime, and explicit DTOs rather than domain entities stay justified whenever another system owns the contract.
pitfalls: Reflection-based serialization of domain entities publishes internal property names and breaks under trimming/AOT; pin explicit DTOs and generate a JsonSerializerContext where AOT matters.
DateTime kind, decimal versus double and dictionary key types do not round-trip by default, so a document that looks valid can come back with shifted timestamps or lost precision.
Deserialize returns null for the JSON literal null and throws JsonException for malformed input, so both paths must be handled explicitly at the endpoint.
Newtonsoft.Json and System.Text.Json attributes are different types; mixing them in one DTO silently ignores half of the configuration.
